data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nighttime heat island is caused by the high emissivity of urban materials, which paradoxically enhances daytime heat absorption and nocturnal release, and the gap is larger in cities with greater building height because the high emissivity surfaces are concentrated in deep street canyons that block longwave loss.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If low-emissivity urban surfaces do not result in lower nocturnal temperatures","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If emissivity variations are shown to be negligible compared to albedo differences","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cross-city gap is independent of the ratio of building height to street width","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Materials like asphalt and concrete have high emissivity, meaning they efficiently emit longwave radiation. While high emissivity should theoretically enhance cooling, the high thermal mass of these materials means they store and conduct heat internally during the day, and the surface temperature remains high. At night, the high emissivity drives strong upward longwave radiation, but the street canyon geometry (building height) reflects this radiation back down, trapping it. The cross-city gap is larger in cities with greater building height because the increased surface area of high-emissivity materials combined with low sky view creates an effective radiative trap.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
